profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an 8-week online graduate module titled "Introduction to Qualitative Research in Education," built around a standard qualitative methods textbook for a new EdD bridge certificate aimed at working K-12 educators. The current proposal includes weekly topics, assignment sketches, sample materials, and a storyboard for the LMS. The agenda is to review whether the proposed module structure, examples, and practice activities are sufficient for the upcoming pilot cohort, identify any gaps in the design, and decide what revisions are needed before handoff to production and faculty approval. The expected outcome is a shared decision on whether the module is "pilot-ready" and a short list of changes to make before launch preparation begins.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Qualitative methodology, ethnographic fieldwork in schools, doctoral curriculum design
members.background: An associate professor in education who has taught introductory qualitative methods for twelve years and previously conducted multi-site school ethnographies; she was asked to adapt her face-to-face course into the new online certificate.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved quickly so the course can clear committee review before her sabbatical, while preserving methodological seriousness and not turning the course into a lightweight skills tutorial.
hidden_assumptions: "Pilot-ready" means the intellectual sequence, readings, and assignments are settled enough for a limited first offering, even if some learner-facing assets are still placeholders.
When a course plan says to include textbook examples, linking learners to the book's appendix or a simple PDF excerpt is normally sufficient unless a special activity is explicitly requested.
"The case study" naturally refers to the shared instructor-provided school case used to give all students common material for early analysis.
Because the certificate targets practicing educators, an "observation session" ordinarily means students observe a real setting available to them and produce fieldnotes from that live encounter.

members.name: Samir Patel
members.expertise: Online course production, LMS architecture, accessibility, adult professional learning design
members.background: A senior instructional designer who has converted many campus courses into online and hybrid formats, especially for working professionals, and is responsible for getting this module through storyboard, media production, and LMS build.
members.private_state: He needs the blueprint stable enough for the production team to start building without scope creep, and he wants to avoid any activities that depend on inconsistent learner access or late faculty-created materials.
hidden_assumptions: "Pilot-ready" means the course can move directly into LMS production with all required learner-facing assets, interaction logic, accessibility notes, and facilitation prompts specified.
If the storyboard says an example is part of instruction, the example needs to be reproduced inside the LMS as an annotated activity rather than left in an external textbook appendix.

"The case study assignment" most naturally refers to the learner's own workplace-based inquiry or the capstone practice task, because that is the main applied deliverable in programs for working educators.

An online module cannot rely on every learner having ethical and practical access to live school observation, so an "observation practice" activity defaults to provided video or simulated materials unless a field placement process is separately defined.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the course is "pilot-ready."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the module is pilot-ready once the conceptual arc, readings, and assignment intentions are approved for a first cohort, with some content assets still to be fleshed out later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the module is pilot-ready only if it is sufficiently specified for immediate LMS build, including exact activity structure, embedded materials, and accessibility-ready asset lists.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both work in environments where "pilot" is a familiar milestone, so the phrase sounds settled and professional; each assumes the other uses the standard meaning from their own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to "use the fieldnotes examples from Appendix B" and to provide a "worked example."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means students will read the textbook appendix and perhaps download one excerpted PDF that she already uses in class.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the examples will be converted into an in-platform annotated exercise where students click through, tag observations, and compare with commentary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase "use the examples" sounds like a simple content inclusion decision, not a boundary-setting decision about whether the material lives in the book, a handout, or a fully built interactive asset.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'case study' they are talking about
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to "the case study" when discussing how students will apply Chapter 2 on research design.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the common Riverview Middle School literacy case that all students analyze early in the module to compare case study and multi-site design choices.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the later workplace-based practitioner inquiry assignment in which each learner frames their own school or classroom as a case.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The proposal uses the phrase "case study" in more than one place, and both are education-appropriate uses; because each participant is focused on a different layer of the design, the shared label creates false consensus.

misalignment_points.topic: How the observation practice will be carried out
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree students should complete an "observation session" and submit fieldnotes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes students will conduct one live 30-minute observation in a real educational setting they already have access to and then write fieldnotes from that experience.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes students will complete the observation practice through provided classroom video clips and artifacts, because access and consent for live observation are too variable for an online pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the level of a design review, both options satisfy the same pedagogical purpose, so the shared phrase "observation session" feels adequately precise even though the execution model differs substantially.

turns.inner_thought: I need this approved before I disappear into sabbatical prep. For me, pilot-ready means the weekly intellectual arc is settled, the readings and assignments make methodological sense, and no one is trying to flatten this into a generic practitioner-skills course. We can still tighten learner-facing pieces afterward if needed. I'll frame this around the sequence so we can move quickly.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I want to do today is confirm that the module is pilot-ready and just walk quickly through the arc week by week—from foundations into fieldwork, then analysis, then the final writing piece—so we can see if anything substantive is still missing.

turns.inner_thought: The sequence is fine; my concern is whether it's actually buildable. Pilot-ready, from my side, means the storyboard is specific enough that production can enter the LMS without guessing at assets, interactions, or accessibility treatments. If there are still fuzzy spots, those become delays and scope creep later.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. From my side, the overall flow looks solid already. What I mostly want to verify is that the storyboard is detailed enough for the pilot build and a clean handoff to production.

turns.inner_thought: Week 3 is where the course starts feeling real. They should do one live observation in a setting they already know—classroom, hallway, meeting, whatever they can access appropriately—write fieldnotes, and then compare what they produced with the fieldnotes examples from Appendix B. A simple excerpt and maybe one worked example will do; I don't need a whole digital apparatus around it.
turns.utterance: Great. In Week 3, the key move is fieldwork practice: students complete an observation session, write fieldnotes, and then compare what they produced with the fieldnotes examples from Appendix B. I do think a worked example there will help them see the difference between noticing and actually recording.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that's a strong online pattern: observation activity, then a structured worked example using the Appendix B fieldnotes right in the course so learners can step through and compare. And if the observation session is standardized through provided media, we can align the example tightly and avoid variability. I should signal that this is straightforward to build without reopening the design.
turns.utterance: I think that will work really well. We can build the worked example so students step through the Appendix B fieldnotes alongside the observation activity, which should make the practice feel much more concrete.

turns.inner_thought: Now Chapter 2. The case study matters because the shared Riverview school case gives everyone common ground before they go off into their own contexts later. If they don't have a common text early, their design comparisons get muddy fast. I need that conceptual anchor protected.
turns.utterance: When we get to Chapter 2, the case study segment is especially important to me because it gives everyone a common basis for thinking through design choices before they branch into their own interests.

turns.inner_thought: Good—that aligns with keeping the applied thread visible early. If the case study helps participants frame their own school or classroom as a site of inquiry from the start, they'll see relevance immediately and stay engaged. That's exactly the kind of authentic connection adult learners want in a bridge certificate.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. I also think the case study will help the course feel immediately relevant, since participants can anchor it in their own school setting pretty early.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want ethics to balloon in the intro module, especially for a low-stakes live observation practice that most educators can manage in familiar settings. We can introduce basic discretion and note-taking boundaries, but this is not the place for a heavy formal review process discussion. If I let that expand, the methods core gets squeezed.
turns.utterance: On ethics, I think we can keep things fairly light in this introductory module, because the observation session is mainly practice and the first pilot cohort are all educators who know school settings.

turns.inner_thought: That works for me. If the observation piece is a contained, standardized practice activity using provided materials, we can keep the instructions brief and avoid a lot of edge-case policy language. That also supports pilot-ready in the production sense: fewer branching contingencies, cleaner build.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. And if we keep the learner instructions concise, the observation piece should be easy to standardize for the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: To keep this moving, I'll just send the Appendix B excerpt I already use and a few short comments about what to notice in it. That should be enough for the worked example without me drafting a lot of new prose. I do not have time to create a whole interactive script before committee review.
turns.utterance: On materials, I can send over the fieldnotes excerpt and a few short comments, and that should cover the worked example without requiring much extra writing.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Once I have the excerpt and her notes, my team can translate that into the interactive pages, write the supporting prompts, and lock the asset list. That's what I need to treat this as pilot-ready for build. Hopefully there aren't more hidden faculty additions after this.
turns.utterance: Great, that helps a lot. Once I have that content, I can slot it into the interactive pages and finalize the asset list for the pilot build.

turns.inner_thought: One thing I need to watch is proportion. The shared case study discussion in the early design week should clarify design logic, not take over the course. We still need enough room later for coding, memoing, and the writing-up piece or the module will lose seriousness.
turns.utterance: The only thing I really want protected is that the case study section not crowd out the analysis and writing weeks later in the module.

turns.inner_thought: I don't see major blockers. If she sends the fieldnotes content and any final notes soon, we can clean up the storyboard and move straight into build on schedule. From my perspective, we're close, as long as those remaining assets arrive in a form production can use.
turns.utterance: That feels very manageable to me. I’m only seeing minor cleanup items, and once I receive your notes, the course should be in good shape for the pilot timeline.
